focus: Exodus 20 records God speaking the Ten Commandments to the people He has just brought out of the house of bondage, first concerning their worship of Him and then concerning their life with one another. The people tremble at His voice and ask Moses to speak for God, and the chapter ends with the opening instructions of the Book of the Covenant: no gods of silver or gold, and an altar where the LORD will come and bless.

sections.title: The LORD Who Brought Israel Out Speaks
sections.summary: God speaks all these words and begins by naming who He is and what He has done: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage” (Exodus 20:2). The commandments that follow are given to a people already redeemed.

sections.title: The Commandments Concerning Israel’s Worship of the LORD
sections.summary: Israel is to have no other gods before the LORD, make no carved image to bow down to, and not take His name in vain, for He is “a jealous God” who shows mercy to thousands who love Him (Exodus 20:5–6). They are to “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8), resting on the seventh day because the LORD rested and hallowed it after creating the heavens and the earth.

sections.title: The Commandments Concerning Life with One’s Neighbor
sections.summary: Israel is to honor father and mother, with the promise of long days in the land. They must not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness against a neighbor, or covet anything that belongs to a neighbor.

sections.title: The People Fear and Moses Draws Near the Thick Darkness
sections.summary: Seeing the thunder, lightning, trumpet, and smoke, the people tremble, stand far off, and ask Moses to speak to them instead of God. Moses tells them, “Do not fear; for God has come to test you, and that His fear may be before you, so that you may not sin” (Exodus 20:20), and he draws near the thick darkness where God is.

sections.title: No Gods of Silver or Gold, and an Altar for the LORD
sections.summary: The LORD reminds Israel that He has spoken with them from heaven and forbids them to make gods of silver or gold to be with Him. He directs them to build an altar of earth or uncut stone without steps and promises, “In every place where I record My name I will come to you, and I will bless you” (Exodus 20:24).

1.brief: “And God spoke all these words.” The commandments come directly from God Himself, spoken to the whole people.
1.explain:
“And God spoke all these words, saying:”

The commandments come directly from God. “God spoke.” Moses did not invent them, and no human council drew them up. The whole people heard God’s voice from the mountain (20:18–19; Deuteronomy 4:12–13; 5:22). Later God wrote them on tablets of stone with His own finger (31:18).
1.notes:
Deuteronomy 4:13 calls them “the Ten Commandments,” literally the ten words. Deuteronomy 5:6–21 repeats them with small differences, especially in the Sabbath command.

This study follows the Reformed numbering. Exodus 20:1–2 introduces the commandments. The first forbids other gods (20:3), the second forbids images (20:4–6), and coveting is one commandment (20:17). Other traditions number them differently.

2.brief: God introduces Himself: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” The commandments are given to a people God has already redeemed, so obedience answers His saving love rather than earning it.
2.explain:
“I am the LORD your God,”

God begins by naming Himself. “I am the LORD,” the covenant name He revealed to Moses (3:14–15; 6:2–3). He is “your God,” bound to Israel by His own choice and promise.

“who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.”

Before giving one command, God reminds Israel what He has done. He “brought you out” of slavery. The commandments are given to a people already redeemed. Israel does not obey in order to be rescued. They obey because they have been rescued. The law is the shape of life for the people God set free. The Reformed tradition, which this study follows, speaks of three uses of the law: it shows sin and leads to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24), it restrains evil in society (1 Timothy 1:9–10), and it guides believers in a life that pleases God (Romans 8:4; 13:8–10). It also distinguishes the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, from Israel’s civil and ceremonial laws, which applied to Israel as a nation and pointed ahead to Christ. The Ten Commandments remain the moral law that still binds believers. Some Christians understand the law differently, teaching that believers are under “the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21; Galatians 6:2) rather than the law of Moses as a whole, while still upholding the moral commands repeated in the New Testament.

3.brief: “You shall have no other gods before Me.” The first commandment calls for exclusive loyalty to the God who rescued them.
3.explain:
“You shall have no other gods before Me.”

The first commandment calls for complete loyalty to the God who rescued them. “No other gods.” The phrase “before Me” can mean in My presence or in addition to Me. Israel must not set any god beside the LORD, much less above Him. Egypt had many gods, and the nations of Canaan would have many more. Israel was to worship the LORD alone. Jesus calls this the first and great commandment in its positive form: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37; Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Anything a person loves, trusts, or serves above God becomes another god. Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

4.brief: Israel must not make a carved image or likeness of anything in heaven, on earth, or in the water. The second commandment forbids representing God with images or worshiping created things.
4.explain:
“You shall not make for yourself a carved image—”

The second commandment (20:4–6) forbids making “a carved image” for worship. The first commandment forbids worshiping false gods. The second forbids worshiping the true God in a false way.

“any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth;”

No “likeness” of anything in creation may be made as an object of worship. The three realms, sky, land, and water, cover everything God made. Moses later explains the reason: Israel saw no form when God spoke from the fire (Deuteronomy 4:15–19). No created thing can represent the Creator.
4.notes: The commandment does not forbid all art. God Himself commanded carved cherubim for the ark and woven figures in the tabernacle curtains (25:18–20; 26:1). What is forbidden is making images to worship or to represent God. The golden calf shows the danger: Israel called a calf the god who brought them out of Egypt (32:4–5).

5.brief: Israel must not bow down to or serve images, for the LORD is “a jealous God,” visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generations “of those who hate Me.” God’s jealousy is His rightful claim on His people’s worship, and the consequences of idolatry continue in families that keep hating Him.
5.explain:
“you shall not bow down to them nor serve them.”

Israel must not “bow down” to images or “serve them.” Bowing and serving describe worship in body and in practice.

“For I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God,”

God gives the reason. He is “a jealous God.” This is not petty envy. It is the rightful zeal of a husband for his wife’s faithfulness. God has redeemed Israel, and He will not share His people’s worship with another. His jealousy is His rightful claim on the people He redeemed.

“visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me,”

God will “visit,” bring judgment on, sin “to the third and fourth generations.” The phrase “of those who hate Me” is important. The judgment falls on families who continue in their fathers’ hatred of God. Idolatry spreads through households, and its consequences continue in families that keep hating Him. Each person still answers for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20).
5.notes: Three or four generations could be alive in one household at the same time. The phrase may picture the whole family living under one roof sharing in the consequences of the head’s idolatry.

6.brief: God shows mercy “to thousands, to those who love Me and keep My commandments.” His mercy far outweighs His judgment, reaching countless generations of those who love Him.
6.explain:
“but showing mercy to thousands, to those who love Me and keep My commandments.”

God’s “mercy” reaches “to thousands.” This may mean thousands of people or thousands of generations (Deuteronomy 7:9). Either way, the contrast with the third and fourth generations is striking. God’s mercy far outweighs His judgment. It rests on those “who love Me and keep My commandments.” Love for God shows itself in obedience (John 14:15).
6.notes: The Hebrew word translated “mercy” is chesed, God’s steadfast covenant love.

7.brief: Israel must not take the LORD’s name in vain, “for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain.” The third commandment guards the honor of the name God revealed to Moses.
7.explain:
“You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain,”

The third commandment guards God’s “name.” To take it “in vain” means to use it emptily, falsely, or carelessly. This includes swearing falsely by His name, using it lightly, or claiming to belong to Him while living as though He did not matter. The name God revealed to Moses (3:14–15) carries His character and must be treated as holy.

“for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain.”

God warns that He “will not hold him guiltless.” Misusing His name is a serious offense, even if people treat it lightly. Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “Hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9). He also warned against careless oaths and taught that a person’s plain word should be trustworthy (Matthew 5:33–37).

8.brief: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” The fourth commandment calls Israel to set apart the day God has already taught them to rest on through the manna.
8.explain:
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”

The fourth commandment (20:8–11) calls Israel to “remember the Sabbath day.” Israel had already learned the Sabbath through the manna (16:23–30). Now God makes it part of His covenant. They are “to keep it holy,” set apart for Him and different from other days.
8.notes: Deuteronomy 5:12 says “Observe the Sabbath day,” and Deuteronomy 5:15 adds a second reason: Israel was a slave in Egypt, and the LORD brought them out.

9.brief: Six days are for labor and all one’s work. The commandment honors ordinary work as part of the rhythm God established.
9.explain:
“Six days you shall labor and do all your work,”

Six days are for “labor.” Work is not a curse to be escaped. It is part of the rhythm God established, and He honors ordinary work as part of life under Him.

10.brief: The seventh day is the Sabbath of the LORD, on which no one in the household, including servants, animals, and strangers, may work. The rest extends to everyone under the household’s care.
10.explain:
“but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the LORD your God.”

The seventh day belongs to God. It is “the Sabbath of the LORD your God.”

“In it you shall do no work: you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your cattle, nor your stranger who is within your gates.”

The rest reaches everyone in the household, from children to servants and even “cattle.” The “stranger” living among Israel also rests. No one could be forced to work while others rested. The rest extends to everyone under the household’s care.

11.brief: In six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and rested the seventh day, “Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and hallowed it.” The Sabbath is grounded in God’s own pattern at creation.
11.explain:
“For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day.”

God gives the reason for the Sabbath. He made everything “in six days” and “rested the seventh day” (Genesis 2:2–3). Israel’s week follows God’s own pattern at creation.

“Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and hallowed it.”

God “blessed” the day and “hallowed” it, set it apart as holy. The Sabbath is grounded in God’s own pattern at creation. This command belongs to the moral law. Jesus called Himself “Lord of the Sabbath” and used the day for mercy and healing (Mark 2:27–28; 3:1–5), and He calls the weary to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28–30). Believers are called to a serious, deliberate weekly rhythm of ceasing from ordinary work and setting time apart to be with Jesus, to remember His deliverance, worship, and receive His rest. Paul leaves believers free about which day they set apart and warns against judging others over observance (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17).
11.notes: Deuteronomy 5:12–15 gives the same commandment with a different reason attached: Israel is to remember that it was a slave in Egypt and that the LORD brought it out.

12.brief: “Honor your father and your mother,” so that your days may be long in the land God is giving. The fifth commandment begins the commands about life with others, starting in the home, and carries a promise.
12.explain:
“Honor your father and your mother,”

The fifth commandment begins the commands about life with others, starting in the home. To “honor” means to give weight to, to respect and value. Children are to treat their parents with respect, obey them while young, and care for them when old.

“that your days may be long upon the land which the LORD your God is giving you.”

The command comes with a promise: “that your days may be long.” A people who honor their parents will be stable and blessed in the land God gives. Paul calls this “the first commandment with promise” and applies it to children in the church (Ephesians 6:1–3). Jesus rebuked those who used religious excuses to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:9–13).

13.brief: “You shall not murder.” The sixth commandment protects human life.
13.explain:
“You shall not murder.”

The sixth commandment protects human life. The Hebrew verb refers to the unlawful killing of a person. People are made in the image of God, and taking a life unjustly is an attack on Him (Genesis 9:6). Jesus taught that anger and contempt toward a brother violate the heart of this commandment (Matthew 5:21–22). John writes that hatred of a brother is murder in the heart (1 John 3:15).
13.notes: The same law that forbids murder also commands the death penalty for certain crimes (21:12) and permits war in some circumstances. The commandment forbids murder, not every taking of life.

14.brief: “You shall not commit adultery.” The seventh commandment guards the faithfulness of marriage.
14.explain:
“You shall not commit adultery.”

The seventh commandment guards the faithfulness of marriage. Adultery breaks the covenant between husband and wife. God designed marriage as a lifelong union (Genesis 2:24), and He protects it. Jesus taught that looking at a woman to lust after her is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:27–28). Hebrews 13:4 says, “Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled.”

15.brief: “You shall not steal.” The eighth commandment protects what belongs to others.
15.explain:
“You shall not steal.”

The eighth commandment protects what belongs to others. Taking what is not yours, whether by force, fraud, or trickery, breaks this command. It also condemns kidnapping, which the law treats as stealing a person (21:16). Paul writes, “Let him who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give him who has need” (Ephesians 4:28).

16.brief: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.” The ninth commandment guards the truth, especially when a neighbor’s life or good name is at stake.
16.explain:
“You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.”

The ninth commandment guards the truth. To “bear false witness” first meant giving false testimony in court, where a lie could cost a neighbor his property, reputation, or life. The command extends to every form of lying that harms another. Paul writes, “Let each one of you speak truth with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25).
16.notes: The law required at least two witnesses for a serious charge and punished a false witness with the penalty he sought for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:15–19).

17.brief: Israel must not covet a neighbor’s house, wife, servants, animals, or “anything that is your neighbor’s.” The tenth commandment reaches beyond outward actions to the desires of the heart.
17.explain:
“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house;”

The tenth commandment reaches beyond outward actions to the desires of the heart. To “covet” means to desire what belongs to someone else, wanting it for yourself.

“you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”

The list covers family, workers, animals, and “anything.” Coveting is often where theft, adultery, lying, and even murder begin. This command shows that God’s law addresses not only what people do but what they want. Paul writes that this commandment showed him his own sin. Without it he “would not have known covetousness” (Romans 7:7). It is a clear example of the law acting as a mirror. Jesus fulfills the law and draws its demands into the heart (Matthew 5:17–28). He sums up the second table in the command to love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:39; Romans 13:9–10).

18.brief: All the people witness the thunder, lightning, trumpet, and smoking mountain, and they tremble and stand far off. God’s holy presence fills them with fear.
18.explain:
“Now all the people witnessed the thunderings, the lightning flashes, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking;”

The narrative returns to the scene at the mountain. The people saw and heard the storm, the trumpet, and the smoke (19:16–19).

“and when the people saw it, they trembled and stood afar off.”

They drew back from the mountain. God’s holy presence fills them with fear.

19.brief: The people ask Moses, “You speak with us, and we will hear; but let not God speak with us, lest we die.” Overwhelmed by God’s voice, they ask Moses to stand between them and God.
19.explain:
“Then they said to Moses, ‘You speak with us, and we will hear;”

The people turn to Moses. They ask him to be their go-between: “You speak with us, and we will hear.”

“but let not God speak with us, lest we die.”

They are afraid that hearing God’s voice directly will kill them. Overwhelmed by God’s voice, they ask Moses to stand between them and God. Deuteronomy 5:28 records that God approved their request: “They are right in all that they have spoken.”

20.brief: Moses tells them, “Do not fear; for God has come to test you, and that His fear may be before you, so that you may not sin.” Moses distinguishes terror from the reverent fear of God that keeps His people from sin.
20.explain:
“And Moses said to the people, ‘Do not fear;”

Moses tells them “Do not fear.” He means they should not be terrified as if God had come to destroy them.

“for God has come to test you, and that His fear may be before you, so that you may not sin.”

Then he explains the right kind of fear. God has come “to test you,” to prove them, and so that “His fear may be before you.” The reverent fear of God is meant to keep them “that you may not sin.” Moses distinguishes terror from the reverent fear of God that keeps His people from sin.
20.notes: Proverbs 1:7 says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” Proverbs 16:6 adds, “by the fear of the LORD one departs from evil.”

21.brief: The people stand far off, “but Moses drew near the thick darkness where God was.” Moses approaches God on the people’s behalf.
21.explain:
“So the people stood afar off,”

The people stay “afar off.”

“but Moses drew near the thick darkness where God was.”

Where the people hold back, Moses goes forward. He approaches God on the people’s behalf, as they asked. Moses serves as the mediator between God and Israel. Paul calls Moses a mediator of the law (Galatians 3:19). Hebrews says believers have come to Jesus, “the Mediator of the new covenant” (Hebrews 12:24). 1 Timothy 2:5 says there is “one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus.”

22.brief: The LORD tells Moses to say, “You have seen that I have talked with you from heaven.” The instructions that follow rest on the fact that God has spoken to them directly.
22.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Thus you shall say to the children of Israel:”

God gives Moses further words for the people. These begin what 24:7 calls “the Book of the Covenant” (20:22–23:33).

“You have seen that I have talked with you from heaven.”

God reminds them of what they witnessed. They heard His voice but saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12, 36). The instructions that follow rest on the fact that God has spoken to them directly.

23.brief: Israel must not make gods of silver or gold to be with the LORD. The first instruction of the Book of the Covenant applies the commandments about worship.
23.explain:
“You shall not make anything to be with Me—gods of silver or gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves.”

The first instruction applies the commandments about worship. Israel must not make “gods of silver or gods of gold” to stand beside the LORD. Having heard the living God speak, they must not turn to idols made by human hands.

24.brief: Israel is to make an altar of earth for burnt offerings and peace offerings, and God promises, “In every place where I record My name I will come to you, and I will bless you.” God, not the worshiper, chooses where He will meet and bless His people.
24.explain:
“An altar of earth you shall make for Me,”

God tells Israel how to build “an altar.” It is to be made “of earth,” simple and natural, not elaborate or costly.

“and you shall sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen.”

On it they will offer “burnt offerings,” wholly burned to God, and “peace offerings,” shared in fellowship with Him.

“In every place where I record My name I will come to you, and I will bless you.”

God chooses where He will be worshiped. “Where I record My name” means where God causes His name to be remembered. In such places He promises, “I will come to you, and I will bless you.” God, not the worshiper, chooses where He will meet and bless His people. The altar is not a means of controlling God’s presence.
24.notes: Deuteronomy 12:5–14 later commands Israel to bring their offerings to the place God would choose to put His name.

25.brief: If Israel builds an altar of stone, they must not build it of hewn stone, for using a tool on it profanes it. Even the way an altar is built must follow God’s instruction.
25.explain:
“And if you make Me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stone;”

If they use stones, the stones must be uncut.

“for if you use your tool on it, you have profaned it.”

Using “your tool” on the stones would “profane” the altar, make it common. The altar must be as God gave the materials, not shaped by human skill. Even the way an altar is built must follow God’s instruction.
25.notes: Joshua built an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal “as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded” (Joshua 8:30–31).

26.brief: Israel must not go up to the altar by steps, so that their nakedness is not exposed on it. Even the way they approach God’s altar must preserve modesty and reverence.
26.explain:
“Nor shall you go up by steps to My altar, that your nakedness may not be exposed on it.”

Israel must not build “steps” up to the altar. Climbing steps in a long robe could expose the body. God’s worship must be marked by modesty and reverence. Later the priests were given linen undergarments for this purpose (28:42–43).
